Havilah
hav'i-lä
n. (a land encompassed by the river Pison in the account of Eden, where there is gold; also the name of two men in the table of nations, and a boundary of the Ishmaelite and Amalekite country)
From Hebrew Chaviylah, probably from chul, to twist or writhe, and taken by some as circle or sandy tract. The name attaches to a Cushite (Gen 10:7) and to a Joktanite (Gen 10:29), and to a region on the desert border between Egypt and Assyria.

Biblical Definition

Havilah is one of the four place-names in the geography of Eden, and the only one Scripture pauses to describe: “The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold” (Gen 2:11), and the following verse adds that the gold of that land is good, with bdellium and the onyx stone. It is a striking notice. Before the fall, before commerce, before any use for currency, Moses tells the reader that there was gold in the world and that it was good gold — created things with worth in them, waiting for men who would either steward or worship them. The name recurs as a Cushite in the sons of Ham: “And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha” (Gen 10:7), and as a Joktanite in the line of Shem (Gen 10:29), so that two peoples of the name existed. As a boundary it marks the run of the Ishmaelite settlements: “they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria” (Gen 25:18), and the same limits define Saul's Amalekite campaign: “And Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur” (1Sa 15:7) — the very war in which he spared Agag and lost the kingdom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Havilah; in sacred history it is a land compassed by the river Pison, where there is gold, and a boundary of the Ishmaelite country.

expand to see more

HAVILAH, n. A land named in the second chapter of Genesis, compassed by the river Pison.

It is said that there is gold in that land, and that the gold is good.

Bdellium and the onyx stone are named there also.

Havilah is likewise the name of a son of Cush and of a son of Joktan.

The seed of Ishmael dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:11 — "The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;"

Gen 10:7 — "And the sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah, and Sabtah, and Raamah, and Sabtecha: and the sons of Raamah; Sheba, and Dedan."

Gen 10:29 — "And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan."

Gen 25:18 — "And they dwelt from Havilah unto Shur, that is before Egypt, as thou goest toward Assyria: and he died in the presence of all his brethren."

Modern Corruption

The land of Eden is commonly treated as mythological geography with no location in the real world. Moses writes it as a map with named rivers and a country known for its gold, and the dictionary reads it as he wrote it.

expand to see more

The standard academic handling of Genesis 2:10-14 is to call it symbolic topography — a paradise-motif dressed in place-names, not a description of anywhere. But the passage does not read like myth. It names four rivers, tells which way each runs, names the countries they compass, and pauses to record the natural products of one of them: gold, and good gold, with bdellium and onyx. That is the diction of a survey. Two of the four rivers, Hiddekel and Euphrates, are ordinary rivers of the known world and are so used everywhere else in Scripture. Moses is locating a real garden in a real world, in terrain the flood afterward wrecked beyond recovery — which is why the site cannot now be found, and is not a reason to conclude there was none.

The doctrinal weight is heavier than a map. If Eden is a symbol, Adam is a symbol, and if Adam is a symbol the whole argument of Romans 5 collapses: “For as by one man&#39;s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). The parallel requires two historical men. Paul builds the resurrection on the same footing: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit” (1Co 15:45). Havilah, gold and all, is one of the small stakes driven into the ground to show that the writer thought he was describing the earth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chaviylah (H2341), Havilah; Piyshon (H6376), Pison, the river; zahab (H2091), gold; bedolach (H916), bdellium; shoham (H7718), onyx stone.

expand to see more

Hebrew Chaviylah (H2341) — Havilah; land, and the name of two men.

Hebrew Piyshon (H6376) — Pison; the first of the four rivers of Eden.

Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold; noted as good in the land of Havilah.

Hebrew bedolach (H916) — bdellium; an aromatic gum, or by some a gem.

Hebrew shoham (H7718) — onyx; later set in the ephod of the high priest.

Usage

"“Compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold” — a map, not a metaphor."

"“The sons of Cush; Seba, and Havilah” — the name borne by a man before a country."

"“From Havilah unto Shur” — the desert boundary of Ishmael and of Amalek."
